client.name: Evergreen City Zoo
client.ask: A public visitor bot and an internal staff assistant.
client.brief:
"We want a friendly assistant on our website that answers visitor questions: tickets, hours, events, accessibility, animal facts. And we want something for our own people, so a new keeper or volunteer can quickly find the right procedure. We're a conservation organization, so whatever you build should reflect our values."

You're the lead AI engineer at Northbound AI Consulting. Evergreen City Zoo is a nonprofit with about 1 million visitors a year, 300 staff and 500 volunteers. Guest services answers about 2,000 repetitive calls and emails a week, and new staff struggle to find procedures spread across binders, PDFs and a shared drive. The first-year budget is $60,000. They want two assistants: a public visitor bot and an internal staff assistant. There's no single winning score: the client has priorities, and you'll only learn all of them if you ask the right questions.

Visitor bot: used by families, tourists, non-English speakers and visitors with disabilities. Questions about prices, hours, parking, access and animal facts. High and spiky traffic.

Staff assistant: used by keepers, vets, guest services, security and volunteers (about 800 users). Questions about feeding, enclosure protocols, emergencies and HR policy. Low and steady traffic.

stakeholders.name: Marketing director
stakeholders.question: Who are your visitors?
stakeholders.answer: About 30% of our visitors prefer Spanish, Mandarin or Vietnamese.
stakeholders.shortAnswer: 30% of visitors prefer a language other than English
stakeholders.reveals: 30% of visitors prefer a language other than English

stakeholders.name: Guest services lead
stakeholders.question: What are your busiest times?
stakeholders.answer: Summer weekends. Traffic is about 8 times a normal weekday.

stakeholders.name: Operations manager
stakeholders.question: What documents would the assistant use?
stakeholders.answer: Website FAQs, plus animal-care manuals. Most manuals are scanned PDFs, many 3+ years old.
stakeholders.shortAnswer: Care manuals are old scanned PDFs
stakeholders.reveals: Care manuals are old scanned PDFs

stakeholders.name: Communications lead
stakeholders.question: Who keeps information up to date?
stakeholders.answer: Nobody owns that. Updates happen when someone notices.

stakeholders.name: IT & security lead
stakeholders.question: What data is sensitive?
stakeholders.answer: Security schedules and HR files sit in the same shared drive as the public FAQs.
stakeholders.shortAnswer: Sensitive files share a drive with public FAQs
stakeholders.reveals: Sensitive files share a drive with public FAQs

stakeholders.name: Head veterinarian
stakeholders.question: What happens if the assistant is wrong?
stakeholders.answer: An outdated feeding or medication protocol could harm an animal.
stakeholders.shortAnswer: Wrong care advice can harm animals
stakeholders.reveals: Wrong care advice can harm animals

stakeholders.name: Accessibility coordinator
stakeholders.question: Do you have accessibility requirements?
stakeholders.answer: Yes. The site must meet WCAG 2.1 AA: screen readers and plain language.

stakeholders.name: Finance director
stakeholders.question: What is your real budget for running costs?
stakeholders.answer: The board caps ongoing costs at $1,500 a month after launch.

stakeholders.name: Executive director
stakeholders.question: How do you measure success?
stakeholders.answer: Fewer calls to guest services, happy visitors, and staff who actually use it.
stakeholders.shortAnswer: Success = fewer calls + satisfaction + staff adoption
stakeholders.reveals: Success = fewer calls + satisfaction + staff adoption

stakeholders.name: Sustainability officer
stakeholders.question: How does this fit your mission?
stakeholders.answer: We publicly report our carbon footprint. The board will ask about energy use.
stakeholders.shortAnswer: Board reports the zoo's carbon footprint
stakeholders.reveals: Board reports the zoo's carbon footprint

rooms.title: Zoo Visitor Center

scene.alt: The zoo entrance: a wooden gate arch reading Evergreen City Zoo, with trees and rolling lawns.

rooms.helperText: You're the lead AI engineer at Northbound AI Consulting. Evergreen City Zoo is a nonprofit with about 1 million visitors a year, 300 staff and 500 volunteers. Guest services answers about 2,000 repetitive calls and emails a week, and new staff struggle to find procedures spread across binders, PDFs and a shared drive. The first-year budget is $60,000. They want two assistants: a public visitor bot and an internal staff assistant. There's no single winning score: the client has priorities, and you'll only learn all of them if you ask the right questions.

rooms.title: Meeting Room

scene.alt: A meeting room with a window over the city, a whiteboard titled Kickoff · Zoo AI Assistants, and a long table.

rooms.goal: Ask up to 6 people one question each.
rooms.helperText: In consulting, the first meeting decides what you know. You can ask 6 of these 10 people one question each, and you can't take a question back. Constraints you don't ask about still exist. You'll just meet them later. Some questions matter much more to this client than others.
rooms.reflectionPrompt: Which question you didn't ask worries you most?

rooms.title: Architecture Studio

scene.alt: A whiteboard sketch of boxes and arrows, with one dashed box still undecided.

rooms.goal: Sketch the system: structure, then models.
rooms.helperText: Decide how the two assistants relate, then pick a model approach for each. Each assistant's model counts for half on the meters, since together they make one design. Cards show typical cost and speed. The full trade-offs appear after you lock in.
rooms.reflectionPrompt: Why might the two assistants need different models?

rooms.title: Records Archive

scene.alt: Floor-to-ceiling shelves of colorful binders and manuals.

rooms.helperText: Your team has 3 effort points this room. Doing every decision well costs 5, so you have to choose where effort matters most. The data you choose decides what each assistant can say, and what it might leak.
rooms.reflectionPrompt: Where did you choose not to spend effort, and who could that affect?

rooms.title: Safety Control Room

scene.alt: A dark control room with a row of monitor screens and a glowing shield.

rooms.goal: Set the guardrails for each assistant.
rooms.helperText: Putting a person on every message would be safe but unaffordable. The skill here is choosing where people add the most value, and treating a public bot differently from a safety-critical staff tool.
rooms.reflectionPrompt: Where does a person add the most value in your design?

rooms.title: Launch Operations

scene.alt: A launch dashboard with a go-live checklist and a rising bar chart.

rooms.goal: Choose how to launch and what to watch.
rooms.helperText: Your launch plan changes how hard problems hit: a pilot surfaces them at smaller scale. Each monitoring tool can catch a matching kind of problem early. You can pick two.
rooms.reflectionPrompt: Which risk on your blueprint are you not watching?

rooms.title: Six Months Later

scene.alt: A wall of pinned newspaper clippings.

rooms.goal: The headlines are in. Respond to each one.
rooms.helperText: Each headline traces back to decisions you made. An emergency fix recovers half the loss but costs budget. Accepting the loss saves money but leaves the damage.

rooms.title: Debrief Gallery

scene.alt: A gallery wall of framed pictures.

rooms.goal: See your design, reflect, and compare.
rooms.helperText: The dashed shape shows what this client needed: 7 on its high priorities (budget, privacy, fairness, accuracy, trust) and 5 on the rest. Compare your blueprint with a sample expert design. The sample is one defensible answer, not the only one.

options.label: One shared system
options.helperText: One knowledge base for both assistants. Simplest and cheapest to build and maintain, but every document is available to both.

options.label: Shared platform, separate data
options.helperText: Shared infrastructure, but role-based access decides which documents each assistant can see.

options.label: Two separate systems
options.helperText: Independent builds, vendors and data stores. Strong separation, but double the cost and maintenance.

options.label: FAQ / rules bot
options.helperText: A decision tree over approved answers. Cheap, fast and private, but it can't handle questions nobody wrote an answer for, or unusual phrasing.

options.label: General cloud LLM
options.helperText: A hosted large model answers from general knowledge, not the zoo's documents. Fluent and multilingual, but it can invent facts, and data leaves the zoo.

options.label: Cloud RAG
options.helperText: Retrieval-augmented generation: the model looks up the zoo's own documents and answers from them, with citations. Grounded, but runs on a paid cloud model.

options.label: Private RAG
options.helperText: Same idea as RAG, using a small open model on servers the zoo controls. Data never leaves. High setup cost, low running cost.

options.label: Hybrid FAQ + RAG
options.helperText: Instant canned answers for the top 50 questions; RAG handles everything else. Absorbs traffic spikes cheaply.

options.label: FAQ / rules bot
options.helperText: A decision tree over approved answers. Cheap, fast and private, but it can't handle questions nobody wrote an answer for, or unusual phrasing.

options.label: General cloud LLM

options.label: Cloud RAG

options.label: Private RAG
options.helperText: Same idea as RAG, using a small open model on servers the zoo controls. Data never leaves. High setup cost, low running cost.

options.label: Hybrid FAQ + RAG
options.helperText: Instant canned answers for the top 50 questions; RAG handles everything else. Absorbs traffic spikes cheaply.

options.label: Everything on the drive
options.helperText: Load the whole shared drive. Fast and nothing is missed, including whatever else lives there.

options.label: Curated + tagged sets
options.helperText: A reviewed public set for visitors and a tagged internal set for staff.

options.label: Use scans as-is
options.helperText: Use the scanned PDFs as they are. No extra work, but many are 3+ years old.

options.label: Digitize + vet review
options.helperText: Digitize the manuals and have the vet team review the top 40 procedures.

options.label: Leave them out
options.helperText: Exclude the manuals. The assistant tells staff to check the binder.

options.label: No owner
options.helperText: Update information when someone notices. No ongoing cost.

options.label: Owner + monthly review
options.helperText: Assign a content owner who reviews hours, prices and events monthly.

options.label: English only
options.helperText: Launch in English. Simplest.

options.label: 3 more languages
options.helperText: Translate the top FAQs into Spanish, Mandarin and Vietnamese, with an LLM fallback for the rest.

options.label: Answer anything
options.helperText: The visitor bot answers any question on any topic. Feels open and friendly.

options.label: Zoo topics only
options.helperText: Stay on zoo topics and politely decline the rest. Predictable and on-brand.

options.label: Best guess
options.helperText: The visitor bot always gives an answer, even when it isn't confident.

options.label: Hand off to a person
options.helperText: Say "I'm not sure" and link to a person on chat or phone. Costs some staff time.

options.label: Answer directly
options.helperText: Fastest for busy keepers. No source shown.

options.label: Always cite
options.helperText: Every answer links to the source procedure, so staff can check it.

options.label: Cite + supervisor
options.helperText: Cite the source, and a supervisor confirms medication and emergency answers. Slower, but a person checks the riskiest answers.

options.label: Look up by name
options.helperText: Visitors can ask about a membership by giving a name. Convenient.

options.label: Require login
options.helperText: Members log in first; the bot never sees payment data. One more step.

options.label: Launch to everyone
options.helperText: Both assistants go live for everyone at once. Fastest impact.

options.label: Pilot first
options.helperText: Staff assistant with 20 keepers first; visitor bot during the off-season.

options.label: Answer reviews
options.helperText: Staff read 50 sampled answers each week, looking for errors and leaks.

options.label: Thumbs-down button
options.helperText: Users flag bad answers on the spot.

options.label: Cost dashboard
options.helperText: Usage and spend tracked against the budget cap.

options.label: Accuracy by language
options.helperText: Shows whether some visitors get worse answers than others.

options.label: Carbon reporting
options.helperText: Energy use feeds the board's sustainability report.

risks.text: Both assistants read from one knowledge base. What stops the public bot from seeing internal files?
Security schedules and HR files are now in the knowledge base.
Anyone who knows a member's name can ask about their account.
The visitor bot answers from general knowledge, not the zoo's documents. It may invent things.
The visitor bot guesses when it isn't sure.

Visitors who don't read English get no help.

reflectionPrompts.text: Did you design the visitor bot and the staff assistant the same way or differently? Why?
Which constraint did you prioritize most, and what did that cost you?
Which consequence surprised you? What earlier decision caused it?
If you rebuilt this system tomorrow, what one change would you make?

debrief.rationale: Shared platform with separate knowledge bases. A hybrid visitor bot absorbs summer peaks cheaply; private RAG keeps staff data in-house. With 3 effort points, it curates documents and gets vet-reviewed manuals right, because animal safety outweighs the rest. It accepts an English-only launch and watches accuracy by language to catch that gap early.
